source_boundary.preserved_question_intent: Design an RPC framework for a stated 100k-OPS/100k-QPS target with millisecond-level calls, preserving the source-mentioned Netty, serialization, service governance and load-balancing concerns while keeping QPS and OPS distinct and treating the throughput/latency target as something to prove by workload-specific measurement rather than a guaranteed property of a framework component.

sources.title: Netty 4.2.0.Final released
anchors: Netty 4.2 is the feature line while 4.1 receives bug fixes for the stated support period
4.2 introduces MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup and separates IO handling through injected handlers
4.2 exposes event-loop instrumentation points such as channel counts and IO-versus-task processing time

sources.title: Netty 4.2 MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup API
anchors: the group handles IO tasks with multiple event-loop threads
the number of event-loop threads is an explicit construction parameter
custom chooser strategies can be used, including utilization-oriented selection in current 4.2 API

sources.title: Netty native transports
anchors: Netty provides platform-specific native transports
native transports expose platform features, can generate less garbage and may improve performance compared with NIO
native transport is a deployment option rather than proof of a fixed latency or throughput number

sources.title: gRPC Performance Best Practices
anchors: reuse channels and stubs where possible instead of repeatedly rebuilding connection state
keepalive can reduce first-call delay after idle periods when configured appropriately
long-lived streaming can avoid repeated per-RPC initiation overhead but changes load-balancing and failure/debugging tradeoffs

sources.title: gRPC Deadlines
anchors: clients should set realistic deadlines based on network/server behavior and validate them with load testing
deadline expiry prevents indefinite waiting and servers should stop unnecessary work after cancellation
deadline propagation can preserve a caller's remaining time budget across downstream calls

sources.title: gRPC Service Config
anchors: client behavior can be governed per target through service configuration
load-balancing policy and per-method call behavior can be configured rather than hard-coded into business call sites
the default pick_first policy is not equivalent to distributing calls across all healthy backends

sources.title: gRPC Health Checking
anchors: gRPC defines a standard health service and client-side health checking can stop sending calls to unhealthy subchannels
streaming health updates are intended to scale better than fleets continuously polling unary health checks
health state affects backend eligibility but is separate from connection keepalive

sources.title: gRPC Flow Control
anchors: flow control prevents a fast streaming sender from overwhelming a receiver
a write handed to the RPC framework is not the same as bytes already being transmitted by the OS
manual synchronous flow-control designs can deadlock if both sides write heavily without reading

sources.title: gRPC Retry
anchors: retry policy is configurable per method with attempt/backoff/status-code controls
retries can add backend and network load and therefore must be budgeted rather than enabled blindly
application-visible side effects still need an idempotency contract when an RPC may be attempted again

sources.title: gRPC Graceful Shutdown
anchors: graceful shutdown stops accepting new calls while allowing in-flight calls a bounded chance to finish
a forced shutdown deadline is still needed so draining cannot last forever
connection/server lifecycle is part of RPC reliability during rollout and failover

claims.text: The 100k QPS/OPS and millisecond-latency wording is a target that must be decomposed by unary/streaming mix, payload size, connection count, serialization cost, business-handler time and latency percentile. Neither Netty nor a serializer supplies a universal 100k or millisecond guarantee; capacity must come from target-environment measurement with headroom.
source_anchors: event-loop instrumentation points expose real processing behavior
reuse channels and stubs where possible
validate realistic deadlines with load testing

claims.text: An RPC data plane can use Netty event loops to multiplex many connections, but blocking serialization extensions, business handlers, disk calls or downstream waits must not monopolize IO event-loop threads. IO-loop utilization/queueing and worker-pool saturation are separate capacity dimensions and should be measured independently.
source_anchors: multiple event-loop threads handle IO tasks

claims.text: Clients should reuse connection/channel state and avoid connect/handshake/setup work on the hot path. Multiplexed or long-lived streams can reduce repeated initiation overhead for suitable traffic, while very long streams change balancing and recovery behavior and therefore cannot be a universal default.
source_anchors: streaming avoids repeated RPC initiation overhead but changes load-balancing and failure tradeoffs

claims.text: Service discovery/name resolution should feed a client routing policy over eligible connections; health checking determines whether a backend should receive new calls, while per-method deadlines bound the caller's latency/resource budget. Load balancing, health and timeout policy belong in framework/service configuration rather than ad-hoc business code.
source_anchors: service config controls load balancing and per-method behavior
client health checks stop sending to unhealthy subchannels
deadline propagation preserves remaining call budget

claims.text: A low-latency RPC framework must not hide unlimited retries. Attempts, retryable failures and backoff require a bounded policy; application methods that may be replayed need an idempotency contract, and any retry or hedging strategy must include its extra backend/network load in capacity calculations.
source_anchors: deadlines limit how long the caller is willing to wait

claims.text: Streaming paths need flow control/backpressure so a fast sender does not turn receiver memory/queues into an unbounded buffer. At framework boundaries, bounded pending-request and executor queues should reject or shed work before queueing delay makes the millisecond SLO impossible; acceptance policy and retries must be coordinated to avoid overload amplification.
source_anchors: flow control prevents overwhelming the receiver
deadlines prevent work from waiting indefinitely

claims.text: A native Netty transport can reduce garbage and improve some workloads, and compact/efficient serialization can reduce CPU and bytes, but both are deployment/profile choices. The design must benchmark representative message distributions and include encode/decode allocation, copy count and payload size in the latency breakdown instead of naming one transport or serializer as an unconditional winner.
source_anchors: native transports may generate less garbage and improve performance
Netty 4.2 changes allocation and IO abstractions, so version/deployment must be bounded

claims.text: During deployment or scale-in, endpoints should leave discovery/health eligibility, stop new calls and drain in-flight RPCs up to a deadline before force-close. Otherwise connection churn and abruptly failed calls can dominate tail latency even if steady-state transport performance is fast.
source_anchors: graceful shutdown drains in-flight calls while refusing new work

writer_constraints: Preserve both source variants: one says 100k OPS and one 100k QPS. Do not silently collapse them. State that the target needs an operation mix before capacity arithmetic is meaningful.

Answer as an RPC framework/system design, not a Netty tutorial. Cover client stub/proxy, codec/protocol, connection/channel management, IO event loops, request correlation/in-flight table, server dispatcher, worker isolation, registry/resolver, load balancing, health and observability.

Make the latency budget explicit as a decomposition: client queue/encode, network, server IO queue/decode, handler/downstream work, encode/network response. Do not promise 'millisecond' without choosing a percentile and target environment.

Use persistent connections and multiplexing where the selected wire protocol supports them; do not create a TCP/TLS connection per call. Mention long-lived streams only as a workload-specific option because they change load balancing and failure recovery.
Keep blocking business/downstream work off IO event-loop threads. Define bounded worker/in-flight queues and overload rejection so queueing does not silently consume the latency budget.

Treat serialization as a versioned negotiated codec/profile. Benchmark bytes, encode/decode CPU and allocations with representative payloads; do not declare Kryo, Protobuf, Hessian or another codec universally fastest without a frozen workload.

Describe discovery/resolution separately from load balancing. Health and outlier signals determine endpoint eligibility; routing policy chooses among eligible endpoints. Avoid claiming a single algorithm is always optimal.
Every RPC needs a deadline/time budget. Retries require a retryable-error policy, attempt/backoff budget and idempotency boundary; do not hide retry storms behind framework defaults.
Cover flow control/backpressure for streaming and bounded queues for unary overload. Define what is rejected, retried, degraded or shed when client/server capacity is exhausted.

Cover connection lifecycle: keepalive/idle policy, reconnect with jitter, graceful drain during deployment, stale endpoints and registry partitions. Keepalive is not the same as application/service health.

Capacity proof must use measured safe per-instance throughput and concurrency under representative payload/business-handler distributions. Include CPU, event-loop utilization, worker saturation, GC/allocation, active connections, in-flight calls and downstream bottlenecks; apply headroom and failure-domain loss before computing instance count.

Observability must include per-method QPS/OPS, success/error codes, P50/P95/P99/P999, client/server queueing, encode/decode time, event-loop lag/utilization, in-flight count, connection churn, retry amplification, endpoint skew and dependency latency.

Do not fabricate Alibaba/ByteDance/CMB production topology, RPC framework internals, node counts, payload sizes, latency numbers or personal project experience. Any numeric example beyond the frozen 100k target must be explicitly illustrative.
